claim: The early nephron is patterned by a gradient in β-catenin activity along the axis of the nephron tubule.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that the early nephron is patterned by a gradient in β-catenin activity along the axis of the nephron tubule.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP reporter mice showing different GFP intensities along the proximal-distal axis of nephrons, as shown in Figure 1 and quantified in Figure 1C.

claim: Modifying β-catenin activity forces cells within nephrons to differentiate according to the imposed β-catenin activity level, causing spatial shifts in nephron segments.
source: By modifying β-catenin activity, we force cells within nephrons to differentiate according to the imposed β-catenin activity level, thereby causing spatial shifts in nephron segments.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments using CHIR99021 and IWR1 to modulate β-catenin activity, resulting in altered nephron segment sizes as shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: The β-catenin signalling gradient interacts with the BMP pathway which, through PTEN/PI3K/AKT signalling, antagonises β-catenin activity.
source: The β-catenin signalling gradient interacts with the BMP pathway which, through PTEN/PI3K/AKT signalling, antagonises β-catenin activity and promotes segment identities associated with low β-catenin activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that inhibition of BMPR or PI3K affects β-catenin activity and nephron segmentation, as demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: Modulating β-catenin activity or PI3K rescues segment identities normally lost by inhibition of Notch.
source: modulating β-catenin activity or PI3K rescues segment identities normally lost by inhibition of Notch.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that co-inhibition of Notch with either β-catenin inhibitors or PI3K inhibitors partially rescues nephron segment development, as shown in Figure 7.

claim: TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP signal intensities show an exponentially decreasing gradient along the nephron axis.
source: The TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP signal intensities showed an exponentially decreasing gradient (R2 = 0.999; n = 11 nephrons) suggestive of a single source and first-order decay of the activating signal (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of GFP signal intensity measurements along the nephron axis, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The GFP intensities in the distal segments differ from those in proximal segments by a minimum of a 15-fold difference to a maximum of a 72-fold difference (mean = 39-fold difference).
source: The GFP intensities measured in the distal segments differed from those in proximal segments by a minimum of a 15-fold difference to a maximum of a 72-fold difference (mean = 39-fold difference; n = 10 nephrons; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP signal intensity in different nephron segments.

claim: Podocytes and their precursors at the extreme proximal end of the nephrons are almost completely devoid of β-catenin activity.
source: we consistently found that the podocytes and their precursors at the extreme proximal end of the nephrons were almost completely devoid of β-catenin activity (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data showing minimal TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP signal in the proximal nephron region, as shown in Figure 1A, B and supplementary figures.

claim: β-catenin phosphorylated at Ser33/Ser37/Thr41 most strongly labels the proximal domain (twofold higher compared to medial and distal).
source: Antibodies for β-catenin that was already tagged for degradation (phosphorylated at Ser33/Ser37/Thr41), most strongly labelled the proximal domain (twofold higher compared to medial and distal, p = 6.2 × 10−5 and 1.2 × 10−4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative antibody staining data showing higher levels of phosphorylated β-catenin in the proximal segment, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Wnt9b, secreted by the ureteric bud, activates a canonical β-catenin-mediated pathway in Six2+ mesenchymal nephron progenitor-cells.
source: Nephrons form during embryonic development, when Wnt9b, secreted by the ureteric bud, activates a canonical β-catenin-mediated pathway in a population of overlying Six2+ mesenchymal nephron progenitor-cells (Kobayashi et al., 2008; Karner et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Das et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi et al., 2008; Karner et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Das et al., 2013).

claim: Wnt4 triggers a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET) in nephron progenitor cells.
source: One of these β-catenin target genes, Wnt4, triggers a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET) (Stark et al., 1994; Kispert et al., 1998) in the nephron progenitor cells and these reconfigure into an epithelial renal vesicle (RV).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Stark et al., 1994; Kispert et al., 1998).

claim: Decreasing β-catenin activity favors the differentiation of the proximal cell identity as seen by an increase in maturation rate of glomeruli.
source: Time-lapse analysis showed that, by decreasing β-catenin activity, we favoured the differentiation of the proximal cell identity as was seen by an increase in maturation rate of glomeruli; in contrast, increased β-catenin activity blocked proximal identity formation and the formation of glomeruli (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data of Wt1+/GFP nephrons treated with IWR1, showing accelerated glomerular maturation, as shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Increased β-catenin activity blocks proximal identity formation and the formation of glomeruli.
source: Time-lapse analysis showed that, by decreasing β-catenin activity, we favoured the differentiation of the proximal cell identity as was seen by an increase in maturation rate of glomeruli; in contrast, increased β-catenin activity blocked proximal identity formation and the formation of glomeruli (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data of Wt1+/GFP nephrons treated with CHIR, showing blocked glomerular formation, as shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Releasing cells from increased β-catenin activity by removing CHIR allows them to resume their development and the proximal identity almost fully recovers.
source: Releasing these cells from increased β-catenin activity, by removing CHIR, allowed them to resume their development (Figure 2E). The proximal identity almost fully recovered and glomerular structures formed at almost the same size as those found in controls, show that the ectopically increased β-catenin activity had been actively suppressing the proximal identity (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing recovery of proximal markers after CHIR removal, as shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Lgr5 expression levels increase at high levels of β-catenin activity.
source: Lgr5 expression levels were increased at high levels of β-catenin activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Lgr5-EGFP expression in kidneys treated with CHIR, as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The number of Lgr5 positive nephrons increases significantly at higher β-catenin activity levels (3.0×; p = 0.05) compared to controls.
source: The number of Lgr5 positive nephrons increased significantly at higher β-catenin activity levels (3.0×; p = 0.05) compared to controls or kidneys with decreased β-catenin activity (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Lgr5-EGFP positive nephrons in time-lapse imaging experiments, as shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: Homozygous Lgr5 mutants display no obvious phenotype in the developing kidney.
source: Homozygous mutants displayed no obvious phenotype in the developing kidney (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Lgr5 EGFP-IRES-CreERT2/EGFP-IRES-CreERT2 homozygous kidneys showing normal segmentation, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing β-catenin mildly increases total nephron lengths (1.17×, p = 0.017) compared to controls.
source: Increasing β-catenin did mildly increase total nephron lengths (1.17×, p = 0.017) compared to controls (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of nephron segment sizes in CHIR-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Increasing β-catenin significantly increases the distal segment length (1.8×, p = 0.0003) and severely reduces the proximal segment (0.2×, p = 1.5 × 10−6).
source: but the distal segment was significantly longer (1.8×, p = 0.0003) and the proximal segment was severely reduced (0.2×, p = 1.5 × 10−6).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of nephron segment sizes in CHIR-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Decreasing β-catenin signalling results in much elongated nephrons (1.7×, p = 1.8 × 10−14).
source: Decreasing β-catenin signalling, on the other hand, resulted in much elongated nephrons (Figure 4B,C: 1.7×, p = 1.8 × 10−14)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of nephron lengths in IWR1-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: A gradual increase in β-catenin activity gives a gradual decrease in proximal identity.
source: To address this, we tested whether a gradual increase in β-catenin activity, which only mildly shifted activity levels away from the normal, would give a gradual decrease in proximal identity as would be expected if identities are β-catenin dosage-dependent. This was observed in nephrons that we exposed to different incremental concentrations of CHIR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using incremental CHIR concentrations showing dose-dependent effects on proximal identity, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mild increase in β-catenin activity promotes expression of most distal segment genes (Wnt4, Pax8, Fgf8, Lhx1, Lgr5).
source: qRT-PCR analysis of RNA from whole treated kidneys confirmed that a mild increase in β-catenin activity promoted expression of most distal segment genes (Wnt4, Pax8, Fgf8, Lhx1, Lgr5) (Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased expression of distal segment markers in CHIR-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Apc+/1638N Ctnnb1+/E654 kidneys develop ectopic nephrons that are positive for Jag1, Cdh1, and laminin but lack podocytes.
source: The ectopic nephrons were found to be positive for Jag1, Cdh1, and laminin but lacked podocytes, as shown by the absence of Wt1 and Podxl signal (Figure 4F,G right panels, respectively)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining of Apc+/1638N Ctnnb1+/E654 kidneys showing ectopic nephrons lacking proximal markers, as shown in Figure 4F, G.

claim: Neither increasing nor decreasing β-catenin signalling levels changes the number of mitotic nuclei per nephron.
source: Neither increasing nor decreasing β-catenin signalling levels changed the number of mitotic nuclei per nephron (Figure 5A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of phosphorylated Histone 3 positive nuclei in nephrons treated with CHIR or IWR1, as shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Blocking cell proliferation with methotrexate (MTX) does not affect the patterning of the nephron.
source: nor did blocking cell proliferation with methotrexate (MTX; Chabner and Young, 1973) affect the patterning of the nephron. Nephrons that formed in MTX were much smaller compared to control nephrons but expressed Cdh1, Wt1, and Jag1 correctly (Figure 5C)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining showing that MTX-treated nephrons maintain correct segment marker expression despite reduced size, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment with neither IWR1 nor CHIR alters apoptosis in the nephrons.
source: Treatment with neither IWR1 nor CHIR altered apoptosis in the nephrons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL and Annexin V assays showing minimal apoptosis in treated nephrons, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: BMP2/4/7 are expressed in the nephron.
source: BMP2/4/7 are expressed in the nephron (Oxburgh et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Oxburgh et al., 2011).

claim: The BMP/SMAD pathway is active in the nephron.
source: and the BMP/SMAD pathway is active (Blank et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Blank et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2013).

claim: BMP pathway activity in the medial segment of the nephron is confirmed using pSMAD1/5/8 reporter BRE-LacZ.
source: We confirmed BMP pathway activity in the medial segment of the nephron using pSMAD1/5/8 reporter BRE-LacZ (Blank et al., 2008) (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by BRE-LacZ reporter expression data showing strong labeling in the medial segment, as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: BRE-LacZ reporter activity closely correlates with the Jag1+ domain.
source: This closely correlated with the Jag1+ domain (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-staining of BRE-LacZ with Jag1 showing overlapping expression patterns, as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Inhibiting BMPR with LDN-193189 results in a rise in the levels of phosphorylated PTEN (inactive) and phosphorylated AKT (active) in nephrons and the ureteric bud.
source: If BMP signals via PTEN, the expected outcome of BMPR inhibition would be a rise in the levels of phosphorylated PTEN (inactive) and phosphorylated AKT (active) (He et al., 2004), which was indeed found in nephrons and the ureteric bud (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining showing increased pPTEN and pAKT levels after LDN-193189 treatment, as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PI3K inhibition reduces β-catenin reporter activity levels in nephrons.
source: Inhibition of PI3K should do the opposite. The total β-catenin reporter activity as measured throughout nephrons, 22 hr after nephron formation, was indistinguishable between controls and BMPR inhibited nephrons, but PI3K inhibition reduced β-catenin reporter activity levels as expected (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP intensity in Ly294002-treated nephrons, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: BMPR inhibition extends high to medium β-catenin reporter activity ectopically into the middle portion of the nephron.
source: This showed that the high to medium β-catenin reporter activity extended ectopically into the middle portion of the nephron when BMPR was inhibited and low levels were detected when PI3K was blocked (Figure 6D,E and Video 8, top part).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing altered β-catenin reporter distribution along the nephron axis after LDN-193189 treatment, as shown in Figure 6D, E.

claim: Inhibiting BMPR and simultaneously activating β-catenin with CHIR synergistically expands β-catenin signalling in the medial nephron segment.
source: Given the observed increase of the β-catenin reporter in response to blocking BMPR, by inhibiting BMPR and simultaneously activating β-catenin with CHIR, this should synergistically expand β-catenin signalling in the medial nephron segment where BMP activity was detected. The ectopic and tree-bound nephrons that formed in these dual-inhibitor conditions displayed very high β-catenin activity throughout the nephron structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and Videos 8, 9, lower part).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP reporter data showing very high β-catenin activity in nephrons treated with both LDN-193189 and CHIR, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Activating β-catenin and inhibiting BMPR at the same time completely removes the Wt1+ cells and strongly reduces the Jag1+ cells.
source: Activating β-catenin and inhibiting BMPR at the same time completely removed the Wt1+ cells, strongly reduced the Jag1+ cells, and formed nephrons made of distal regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining showing loss of proximal and medial markers in kidneys treated with both CHIR and LDN-193189, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Inhibiting PI3K strongly promotes the development of the Jag1+ segment.
source: Inhibiting PI3K on its own strongly promoted the development of the Jag1+ segment and inhibiting BMPR had a slight negative effect on the Jag1+ segment as expected, the latter perhaps partially hidden by the overall increase in nephron length (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining and quantification showing increased Jag1+ segment size in Ly294002-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Inhibiting PI3K positively affects medial markers Dll1, Jag1, Irx2, and Fgf8, and distal marker Lhx1.
source: qRT-PCR analyses on segment-specific genes confirmed that inhibiting PI3K had a positive effect on the medial domain; medial markers Dll1, Jag1, Irx2, and Fgf8 increased, as did distal marker Lhx1 (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased expression of medial and distal markers in Ly294002-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 6G.

claim: β-catenin phosphorylated at Ser552 is localized primarily to the apical surfaces of the nephrons in the distal and medial segments.
source: β-catenin phosphorylated at Ser552 was localised primarily to the apical surfaces of the nephrons in the distal and medial segments (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining showing p-β-catenin Ser552 localization in nephrons, as shown in Figure 6H.

claim: 80% of cells with phosphorylated Ser552 β-catenin at lateral and basal surfaces are found in the distal and medial segments.
source: In a subset of cells, the phosphorylated Ser552 β-catenin was detected at lateral and basal surfaces. 80% of such cells were found in the distal and medial segments (45/56 positive cells counted in five nephrons) and the remaining 20% in proximal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of p-β-catenin Ser552 localization in nephron cells.

claim: Notch-signalling specifies the proximal and medial identity.
source: To date, the only other major pathway known to control nephron patterning is the Notch-signalling pathway (Cheng et al., 2007). Notch-signalling specifies the proximal and medial identity, but it can also block the adjacent glomerular identity when over-activated in these cells (Cheng et al., 2007; Boyle et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cheng et al., 2007; Boyle et al., 2011).

claim: Inhibiting Notch using DAPT results in a loss of proximal and medial structures and glomerular precursors.
source: We first inhibited Notch using the γ-secretase DAPT as previously published (Cheng et al., 2003). This resulted in a loss of proximal and medial structures and glomerular precursors (positive for Podxl and Lotus tetragonolobus lectin (LTL), Figure 7A)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining showing loss of proximal and medial markers in DAPT-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Co-inhibition of β-catenin and Notch-signalling results in the reappearance of nephrons positive for LTL and Podxl that display glomerular structures and medial and proximal development.
source: Co-inhibition of β-catenin and Notch-signalling resulted in the reappearance of nephrons positive for LTL and Podxl that displayed glomerular structures and medial and proximal development (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining showing rescue of proximal markers in kidneys treated with both DAPT and IWR1, as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The inhibition of β-catenin does not restore the expression of key Notch target genes (Jag1, Dll1, Heyl, Hey1).
source: The inhibition of β-catenin did not restore the expression of key Notch target genes (Jag1, Dll1, Heyl, Hey1) (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing that Notch target genes remain downregulated in kidneys treated with both DAPT and IWR1, as shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Co-inhibition of PI3K and Notch results in a partial rescue of the medial segment.
source: Co-inhibition of PI3K and Notch also resulted in a partial rescue (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and Videos 10, 11). Wt1+ cells were not evident but Jag1 was again expressed, indicating that PI3K exerts an effect specific to the medial segment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining showing reappearance of Jag1+ cells in kidneys treated with both DAPT and Ly294002, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Inhibition of Notch results in stunted nephrons without Wt1+ or Jag1+ cells with medium to high level of β-catenin activity throughout.
source: Inhibition of Notch resulted in stunted nephrons without Wt1+ or Jag1+ cells with medium to high level of β-catenin activity throughout (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B–C; Video 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP reporter data and immunofluorescent staining in DAPT-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Maximal activation of β-catenin is incompatible with MET.
source: Previous genetic approaches to investigate the role of β-catenin during nephron formation have been hampered by the problem that when β-catenin is maximally activated in nephron progenitors MET is concurrently blocked (Kuure et al., 2007; Park et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kuure et al., 2007; Park et al., 2007).

claim: MET is only incompatible with very high levels of β-catenin activity.
source: Our data, however, suggest that MET is only incompatible with very high levels of β-catenin activity (Figure 4D and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2), therefore identifying a dose–response correlation between β-catenin activity and renal MET.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that moderate increases in β-catenin activity permit nephron formation while very high levels block it, as shown in Figure 4D and Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2.

claim: Ectopic nephrons form at the periphery of kidneys when β-catenin signalling is increased.
source: Increased β-catenin signalling induced ectopic nephrons to form at the periphery of the kidneys and large nephron structures developed within the ureteric tree (Figure 2—figure supplements 1,2).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing ectopic nephron formation in CHIR-treated kidneys, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2.

claim: Ectopic structures in CHIR-treated kidneys are derived from Six2+ nephron progenitors.
source: Third, we demonstrated that these ectopic structures, just like the tree-bound structures, were derived from Six2+ nephron progenitors by fate-mapping these using a Six2-CreGFP (Dolt et al., 2013) and a Rosa26tdRFP Cre reporter mouse model (Luche et al., 2007) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing experiments using Six2-CreGFP and Rosa26tdRFP reporter mice, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: ICG001, which binds CBP and prevents β-catenin/CBP interaction, inhibits CHIR-induced ectopic nephron formation.
source: Fourth, since pharmacological inhibitors can have multiple targets, we confirmed their specificity by combining activators and inhibitors of the WNT-pathway. Pax8-Cre lineage tracing and immunofluorescent analyses allowed us to show that by blocking β-catenin signalling downstream of GSK-3β (by administering ICG001 which binds CBP and prevents β-catenin/CBP interaction), but not upstream (IWR1), CHIR-induced ectopic nephron formation was inhibited (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that ICG001 blocks CHIR-induced ectopic nephron formation, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: BIO (GSK3β inhibitor) induces effects similar to CHIR.
source: Fifth, additional inhibitors against components of the β-catenin/Canonical WNT-pathway also confirmed our findings: (BIO (GSK3β inhibitor) induced effects similar to CHIR; salinomycin (LRP6 inhibitor) induced effects similar to IWR1 (Gandhirajan et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2011); Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using BIO showing similar effects to CHIR on nephron formation, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Salinomycin (LRP6 inhibitor) induces effects similar to IWR1.
source: Fifth, additional inhibitors against components of the β-catenin/Canonical WNT-pathway also confirmed our findings: (BIO (GSK3β inhibitor) induced effects similar to CHIR; salinomycin (LRP6 inhibitor) induced effects similar to IWR1 (Gandhirajan et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2011); Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using salinomycin showing similar effects to IWR1 on nephron formation, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: In the intestine, BMP negatively regulates β-catenin signalling by inhibiting the PTEN/PI3K/AKT pathway.
source: In the intestine BMP negatively regulates β-catenin signalling by inhibiting the PTEN/PI3K/AKT pathway to maintain high levels of active GSK3β (He et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (He et al., 2004).

claim: Notch2−/− nephrons form no proximal tubules or glomeruli.
source: Notch2−/− nephrons form no proximal tubules or glomeruli (Cheng et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Cheng et al., 2007).

claim: Ectopic expression of the intracellular and active Notch1-domain (N1ICD) in nephrons blocks glomerular development.
source: However, ectopic expression of the intracellular and active Notch1-domain (N1ICD) in nephrons blocks glomerular development (Cheng et al., 2003, 2007; Boyle et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cheng et al., 2003, 2007; Boyle et al., 2011).

claim: N1ICD expression in Six2+ cells can substitute for Wnt9b and trigger nephron induction and MET.
source: N1ICD expression in Six2+ cells can actually substitute for Wnt9b and trigger nephron induction and MET (Boyle et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Boyle et al., 2011).

claim: Wnt9b acts via the planar cell polarity pathway and controls the orientation of cell division and the elongation of collecting tubules.
source: Post-MET, Wnt9b acts via the planar cell polarity pathway and controls the orientation of cell division and the elongation of collecting tubules (Karner et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Karner et al., 2009).

claim: Wnt7b controls the development of the medulla and papilla of the kidney.
source: Wnt7b also has a role as it controls the development of the medulla and papilla of the kidney (Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Yu et al., 2009).

claim: A Wt1+ cell population gives rise to proximal structures in the nephron.
source: Several distinct cell-populations form and these produce the different segments of the adult nephron (Saxen, 1987); a Wt1+ cell population gives rise to proximal structures, a Jag1+ population to the medial part and Lgr5+ cells generate the distal nephron segments (Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Saxen, 1987; Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).

claim: A Jag1+ population gives rise to the medial part of the nephron.
source: Several distinct cell-populations form and these produce the different segments of the adult nephron (Saxen, 1987); a Wt1+ cell population gives rise to proximal structures, a Jag1+ population to the medial part and Lgr5+ cells generate the distal nephron segments (Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Saxen, 1987; Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).

claim: Lgr5+ cells generate the distal nephron segments.
source: Several distinct cell-populations form and these produce the different segments of the adult nephron (Saxen, 1987); a Wt1+ cell population gives rise to proximal structures, a Jag1+ population to the medial part and Lgr5+ cells generate the distal nephron segments (Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Saxen, 1987; Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).

claim: The Wnt4 driven MET is most likely mediated by the non-canonical Ca2+–NFAT pathway.
source: The initiation of the nephron MET is driven by β-catenin signalling (Kobayashi et al., 2008; Karner et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012), but the Wnt4 driven MET is most likely mediated by the non-canonical Ca2+–NFAT pathway (Burn et al., 2011; Tanigawa et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Burn et al., 2011; Tanigawa et al., 2011).

claim: The initiation of the nephron MET is driven by β-catenin signalling.
source: The initiation of the nephron MET is driven by β-catenin signalling (Kobayashi et al., 2008; Karner et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi et al., 2008; Karner et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012).

claim: Notch signalling is important for the formation of the proximal tubule.
source: Notch signalling has previously been identified as being important for the formation of the proximal tubule (Cheng et al., 2003, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cheng et al., 2003, 2007).

claim: Lgr5 is an R-spondin receptor and mediates β-catenin signalling.
source: Lgr5 is also an R-spondin receptor and mediates β-catenin signalling (de Lau et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (de Lau et al., 2011).

claim: Lgr5 knockouts have no phenotype in the intestine.
source: This is maybe not surprising as Lgr5 knockouts have previously been shown to be without phenotype in the intestine where it is an important marker of intestinal stem cells (de Lau et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (de Lau et al., 2011).

claim: In Sertoli cells, Wt1 limits β-catenin activation.
source: A plausible candidate for preventing β-catenin activity in this segment would be Wt1, as in in Sertoli cells Wt1 was shown to limit β-catenin activation (Chang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Chang et al., 2008).

claim: Patterned S-shaped body nephrons form from mesenchymal progenitors within a 24 hr time-span.
source: Since patterned S-shaped body nephrons form from mesenchymal progenitors within a 24 hr time-span, to conditionally knock out Wnts, it would be necessary to identify potential Cre-driving genes that are expressed at the very earliest stages of nephrogenesis but which are not active prior to nephron formation, since deletion at that time-point is likely to block the process.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' observations of nephron development timing.

claim: A gradient of recombinant XWnt8 can drive anterior–posterior neural patterning in dissociated Xenopus embryos with a corresponding gradient of β-catenin activity.
source: In previous studies, a gradient of recombinant XWnt8 has been shown to be able to drive anterior–posterior neural patterning in dissociated Xenopus embryos with a corresponding gradient of β-catenin activity (Kiecker and Niehrs, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Kiecker and Niehrs, 2001).

claim: A gradient in nuclear β-catenin was described in the patterning of the segmentation clock that controls somitogenesis.
source: Similarly, a gradient in nuclear β-catenin was described in the patterning of the segmentation clock that controls somitogenesis (Aulehla et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Aulehla et al., 2008).

claim: The canonical Wnt signalling pathway is known to have a direct effect on cell proliferation.
source: The canonical Wnt signalling pathway is known to have a direct effect on cell proliferation (Davidson and Niehrs, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Davidson and Niehrs, 2010).

claim: Very low levels of apoptosis were detected, primarily at the periphery of the kidneys, in line with previous data.
source: Only very low levels of apoptosis were detected, primarily at the periphery of the kidneys, in line with previous data (Foley and Bard, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL and Annexin V assay data and citation to a previous study (Foley and Bard, 2002).

claim: In many tissues, Notch and Wnt pathways act both in synergy and in opposition.
source: In many tissues, Notch and Wnt pathways act both in synergy and in opposition (Andersson et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Andersson et al., 2011).

claim: Notch antagonises the PTEN/PI3K/AKT pathway in clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma.
source: and Notch has also been reported to antagonise the PTEN/PI3K/AKT pathway in clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Liu et al., 2013).

claim: β-catenin activity levels are selected for by different types of cancer.
source: The series of different Apc and Ctnnb1 mouse models that we employed have previously been used to show that β-catenin activity levels are selected for by different types of cancer, and these ectopic increases in signalling activity can also lead to a range of developmental defects (Kielman et al., 2002; Gaspar et al., 2009; Buchert et al., 2010; Bakker et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kielman et al., 2002; Gaspar et al., 2009; Buchert et al., 2010; Bakker et al., 2013).

claim: LiCl, which is an inhibitor of GSK3β, can induce nephron formation but also blocks MET at high concentrations.
source: It has been known for a long time that LiCl, which is an inhibitor of GSK3β, can induce nephron formation but it also blocks MET at high concentrations (Davies and Garrod, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Davies and Garrod, 1995).

claim: The PI3K pathway has been shown to alter Wnt signalling in embryonic stem cells.
source: The significance of PI3K signalling in connection with Wnt/β-catenin pathway is strongly debated (Ng et al., 2009), but the PI3K pathway has not only been shown to alter Wnt signalling in the gut but also in embryonic stem cells (Paling et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Paling et al., 2004).

claim: AKT phosphorylates β-catenin at Ser552.
source: We tested whether β-catenin was phosphorylated at Ser552 as it has been reported to be by AKT (Fang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Fang et al., 2007).

claim: Proximal and medial nephron cells require Notch signalling and simultaneously need β-catenin and PI3K signalling to be kept at low levels, respectively.
source: Together, these data show that proximal and medial nephron cells require Notch signalling and simultaneously need β-catenin and PI3K signalling to be kept at low levels, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rescue experiments showing that reducing β-catenin or PI3K activity can partially rescue Notch inhibition phenotypes.

claim: Changes in proliferation and apoptosis are not the driving force behind the β-catenin signalling gradient or the patterning of the nephron.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that changes in proliferation and apoptosis are not the driving force behind the β-catenin signalling gradient or the patterning of the nephron.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that modulating proliferation or apoptosis does not affect nephron patterning.

claim: Increasing and decreasing β-catenin signalling changes segmentation by forcing cells to change their identity.
source: Together, these findings would therefore suggest that increasing and decreasing β-catenin signalling changes segmentation by forcing cells to change their identity and that this is the most likely mechanism underlying the alterations to segmentation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that β-catenin modulation affects segment identity without affecting proliferation or apoptosis.

claim: The positional identities in the nephron can be modified through BMP mediated PI3K/AKT signalling.
source: These data indicate that the positional identities in the nephron can be modified through BMP mediated PI3K/AKT signalling and that simulated increased BMP signalling (via inhibition of PI3K) leads to reduced β-catenin signalling, whereas simulated decreased BMP signalling (via inhibition of BMPR) results in the opposite effect.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that BMP/PI3K pathway modulation affects β-catenin activity and nephron segmentation.

claim: Simulated increased BMP signalling (via inhibition of PI3K) leads to reduced β-catenin signalling.
source: These data indicate that the positional identities in the nephron can be modified through BMP mediated PI3K/AKT signalling and that simulated increased BMP signalling (via inhibition of PI3K) leads to reduced β-catenin signalling, whereas simulated decreased BMP signalling (via inhibition of BMPR) results in the opposite effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that PI3K inhibition reduces β-catenin reporter activity.

claim: Simulated decreased BMP signalling (via inhibition of BMPR) results in increased β-catenin signalling.
source: These data indicate that the positional identities in the nephron can be modified through BMP mediated PI3K/AKT signalling and that simulated increased BMP signalling (via inhibition of PI3K) leads to reduced β-catenin signalling, whereas simulated decreased BMP signalling (via inhibition of BMPR) results in the opposite effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that BMPR inhibition increases β-catenin reporter activity.

claim: The observed phenotypes are due to a direct effect on the nephrogenic lineage rather than an indirect effect via the ureteric bud.
source: To test if the observed phenotypes were due to a direct effect on the nephrogenic lineage or an indirect effect via the ureteric bud, we isolated metanephric mesenchyme away from the ureteric bud, induced it to form nephrons with spinal cord (Grobstein, 1953, 1955), and modulated β-catenin activity therein. Comparable to the phenotype observed in whole kidney rudiments, we found that inhibition of β-catenin activity favoured patterning towards the proximal fate, whereas increasing its activity had the opposite effect (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using isolated mesenchyme showing similar effects of β-catenin modulation as in whole kidneys, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The mechanism for the rescue of Notch inhibition phenotypes by β-catenin or PI3K inhibition is by reduction of the level of β-catenin signalling.
source: In common to inhibition of β-catenin and PI3K was that they both decreased β-catenin signalling in nephrons and positively affected the development of the proximal-most and medial segments, respectively. Inhibition of β-catenin signalling in Notch-inhibited nephrons reduced the level of β-catenin signalling and rescued the proximal-most cells whilst co-inhibition of Notch and PI3K partially rescued the medial segment. It is therefore tempting to speculate that the mechanism for these rescues is by reduction of the level of β-catenin signalling.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation/inference from the observation that both β-catenin and PI3K inhibition reduce β-catenin signalling and rescue Notch inhibition phenotypes.
